600:
Austen's first sentence is a joke that takes a second to land. It sounds like a general law, and then "in want of a wife" quietly swaps the subject: the truth is not about what single men need but about what the neighbourhood wants for its daughters. By the end of the paragraph the "rightful property" language has made the families, not the bachelor, the ones being observed.

Pride and Prejudice appeared in January 1813 from Thomas Egerton, credited only to "the Author of Sense and Sensibility". Austen had drafted an earlier version in the 1790s under the title First Impressions, and her father had offered it to a publisher, who turned it down without asking to see it. The finished novel was reworked years later, and the sparring, mostly conversational opening chapter, with Mrs Bennet chattering and Mr Bennet refusing to be impressed, shows how much of the book Austen builds out of dialogue.

A detail worth noticing: Mr Bennet's reply, "You want to tell me, and I have no objection to hearing it," gives away the whole marriage in one line.

If you like this register, read Emma next, where the irony is turned on a heroine instead of her mother.
601:
Three words, and the narrator has already declined to tell you who he is. "Call me Ishmael" is an instruction, not an introduction. It does not say "my name is Ishmael", and many readers have taken that as a hint that the name is chosen. It is also the name of the biblical outcast, which fits a man who says he goes to sea whenever he feels grim about the mouth.

Most editions put several pages in front of this line, a section on the etymology of the word "whale" and a long run of quotations about whales, which Melville assembled from the Bible, poets, sailors and natural histories. The story proper starts after all that, so the sentence arrives as a relief.

Moby-Dick came out in London in October 1851 as The Whale and in New York a month later under the title we know. It sold poorly, and Melville was largely out of print and out of fashion when he died in 1891. Its reputation was built in the 1920s and after.

The first chapter is called "Loomings", and it is gentler than you might expect. For another Melville, try the short story "Bartleby, the Scrivener".
602:
Look at what Dostoevsky leaves out. The young man has no name yet, the street is "S. Place", the bridge is "K. bridge". Readers of the time, and commentators since, have generally decoded these as Stoliarny Lane and the Kokushkin Bridge in St Petersburg, but the novel withholds them, and the effect is a story that begins somewhere deliberately blurred.

What the sentence does tell you is the weather and the mood: an exceptionally hot evening, a man walking "as though in hesitation". The heat matters. Petersburg in July is dusty and airless in the book, and the discomfort feeds the feverish state of the character, Raskolnikov, over the next few days.

Crime and Punishment ran in the journal The Russian Messenger through 1866 and was published as a book soon after. Dostoevsky was writing against debts, and the novel was one of the pieces that rebuilt his career after years in Siberian exile.

The opening has no violence in it, but the garret, the hesitation, and the hint of a plan he is trying not to think about set up the dread.

Next, try Notes from Underground (1864), shorter and angrier, from the same period.
603:
"To Sherlock Holmes she is always the woman." That is the first line of "A Scandal in Bohemia", the opening story of The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, which was published in The Strand Magazine in July 1891 and collected in book form in 1892. In this puzzle the name is hidden, which is the only reason the sentence is hard to place.

The line is doing two jobs. It introduces Irene Adler, and it tells you something unexpected about Holmes: the cold reasoner of the series is allowed to admire one person above everyone else. Watson, who narrates, hurries to say that this is not love, since Holmes, he claims, would find that emotion distasteful in a precise mind. The reader is invited to doubt him.

A detail many readers do not expect: Irene Adler appears in only this one story. Her place in the legend, and in later adaptations, is far larger than her page count.

The story is short enough to read in a sitting, and it is a fair introduction to the series, with a king, a photograph, and a disguise or two. Doyle wrote it in a plain, brisk style, with little scene setting.

After it, read The Sign of the Four for a longer case with a stronger romantic thread for Watson.
604:
The first sentence sets up a joke that the whole book then makes good on. Alice is bored on a riverbank, and the book her sister is reading has "no pictures or conversations in it", which makes her wonder what use a book is. Lewis Carroll's own book is full of both. Characters, mostly, talk back, and the illustrations are by John Tenniel.

Carroll was the pen name of Charles Dodgson, a mathematics lecturer at Christ Church, Oxford. He first told the story on a boat trip on the Thames in 1862 to the daughters of the college's dean, including ten-year-old Alice Liddell, and wrote it out for her as a manuscript, "Alice's Adventures Under Ground". The published version, from Macmillan in 1865, is longer and has new episodes such as the Mad Tea-Party.

In this puzzle the heroine's name is hidden, which turns the first line into a plain description of a child, so it can look generic until the rabbit shows up in the next paragraph.

Much of the book is parody of the moral verses Victorian children were made to learn. Reading it with that in mind helps explain the odd poems.

The sequel, Through the Looking-Glass, is the natural next step.
605:
Frankenstein does not begin with a laboratory. It begins with a letter. Captain Robert Walton, on an Arctic voyage, is writing to his sister in England to say that nothing has gone wrong yet. The monster, and Victor Frankenstein, arrive later, inside Walton's account, and the creature's own story sits inside Victor's. The book is a set of nested narrations, each one a reason to wonder how reliable the next is.

Mary Shelley began it in the summer of 1816, at a villa near Lake Geneva, when bad weather kept her party indoors. Her companions included her future husband Percy Shelley, Lord Byron and Byron's physician John Polidori, and they agreed to each write a ghost story. She was eighteen when she started it, and the first edition appeared anonymously in three volumes in January 1818. The version most people read today is based on her 1831 revision, but the Gutenberg text here is the earlier, more rugged one.

The opening line is a sentence of reassurance that readers know to distrust, because the title has already promised something else. Walton's cheer is the calm before the book.

For more of her work, try The Last Man (1826), a novel about the end of the human race.
606:
This is not a first line so much as a spoiler. Before the play begins, a Chorus steps out and delivers fourteen lines in the form of a sonnet that tell the audience exactly what will happen: two feuding families, two lovers who die, and their deaths ending the feud. The prologue even calls them "star-cross'd".

What does that do to a play? It removes the question of what, and puts the audience's attention on how and why. The tension in Romeo and Juliet is not suspense, but the dread of watching people move toward an outcome you have been told about. Shakespeare repeats the trick in miniature elsewhere in the play, as the characters keep predicting their own ends in ordinary conversation.

The play was first printed in 1597 in a short quarto, which scholars call a "bad quarto" because its text differs from, and is shorter than, the version printed in 1599. It is mostly the later text that readers know.

Shakespeare did not invent the story. He worked from a long English poem, The Tragicall Historye of Romeus and Juliet, by Arthur Brooke, published in 1562.

If you want a Shakespeare comedy afterwards, A Midsummer Night's Dream uses a similar young-lovers plot with a very different result.
607:
Dracula begins as a travel diary, and a dull one on purpose. Jonathan Harker, a young English solicitor, notes the date, the town, the train times and, a few lines later, what he had for dinner. The good-humoured detail makes the later horror feel like an intrusion into a well-kept record.

That choice follows from how the novel is built. Bram Stoker tells the story entirely in documents: journals, letters, telegrams, newspaper cuttings and phonograph recordings. Nobody narrates the whole thing, and the reader has to assemble events from different, partial sources. Harker's opening entry starts in Munich and arrives at Bistritz, the Transylvanian town now spelled Bistrița and part of Romania.

Stoker, an Irish writer, spent most of his working life managing the Lyceum Theatre in London for the actor Henry Irving, and he wrote Dracula in his spare time. It was published by Archibald Constable in 1897. It was well reviewed but did not become a sensation immediately. Its place in popular culture grew mostly through the stage and film adaptations of the 1920s.

Notice that even the train arrives late. Small irritations are the way the book teaches you to trust Harker.

For an older vampire story, read Sheridan Le Fanu's novella Carmilla (1872).
608:
The title promises a monster and the opening gives you a lawyer. The first words of The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde describe Mr Utterson, "cold, scanty and embarrassed in discourse", and a man who is "somehow lovable" in spite of it. The story is told through his eyes: a respectable, uncurious witness to a puzzle he keeps trying not to look at.

That choice is why the book still works. Because Utterson narrates, the reader sees Jekyll from outside for most of the novella and learns what he has been doing only near the end, in two written confessions. Stevenson keeps the structure of a detective story and moves its solution into the reader's head late.

Robert Louis Stevenson wrote it in the mid-1880s while living in Bournemouth, in poor health, and it was published by Longmans, Green in January 1886. He later wrote that the central idea came to him in a dream. The book is short, which makes it one of the easiest classics to finish in a day.

The setting is a foggy, gaslit London of respectable doors and bad habits.

For something more adventurous from the same author, try Kidnapped (1886).
609:
Forster starts in the middle of a complaint. Miss Bartlett is annoyed, someone called the Signora has failed, and we are not told what she has failed at. A few lines on, it is clear that the rooms in a Florentine pension were promised to have views, and don't. The novel is called A Room with a View, so the subject is announced through grumbling.

The first line also introduces the book's central comic engine, the chaperone. Miss Bartlett is Lucy Honeychurch's older cousin, who is travelling with her as a guardian and who keeps finding reasons to turn a trip to Italy into an exercise in propriety. Everything that follows, including a kiss in a field of violets and a retreat to Surrey, is a contest between caution and what Lucy actually wants.

E. M. Forster published it in 1908. He had drafted early versions several years before, after travelling in Italy with his mother, and it was his third novel. The 1985 Merchant Ivory film made it more widely known later in the century.

A small test of Forster's style: he can make a squabble over bedrooms into a political argument without raising his voice.

Read Howards End (1910) next, which has bigger ideas and a similar tone.
610:
"Miss Brooke had that kind of beauty which seems to be thrown into relief by poor dress." The sentence is about clothing, but it quietly characterises Dorothea Brooke: her plain way of dressing is a choice, tied to a serious, slightly ascetic temperament, and the narrator treats it as the thing that makes her stand out in a provincial town where everyone else watches fashion.

Middlemarch is the long novel of the group around her, set in a Midlands town between 1829 and 1832, just before the first Reform Act. George Eliot, the pen name of Mary Ann Evans, published it in eight instalments from December 1871 to December 1872, with the subtitle "A Study of Provincial Life". Before this first sentence most editions have a short prelude about St Theresa, and the Gutenberg text has the same.

Virginia Woolf's remark that it is "one of the few English novels written for grown-up people" has been quoted so often that it can obscure how readable the book is. The first chapter, with its two sisters dividing their mother's jewels, is domestic and quick.

It rewards patience. Each character has a plan for how to be good, and the town tests every one.

If you want a shorter Eliot, try Silas Marner (1861).
611:
"There was no possibility of taking a walk that day." It is a negative sentence, and a wet, cold one. Charlotte Brontë opens with something Jane cannot do. The reader is put inside a house, a child excluded from the family fire, before any plot has started.

The scene that follows sets up the whole novel in small. Ten-year-old Jane retreats behind a curtain with Bewick's History of British Birds, whose pictures of Arctic wastes she studies, and is found by her cousin John Reed, who throws the book at her. That outburst sends her to the red-room, and from there to Lowood school. The abuse and the reading are both part of Jane's character: she learns early that books are somewhere to go and that her anger has consequences.

Jane Eyre was published in October 1847 by Smith, Elder & Co. as "an autobiography, edited by Currer Bell". Brontë used a male-sounding pseudonym, and the novel's first-person voice, plain and direct, was seen as striking in its day.

The book is often remembered for Thornfield Hall, but its first chapter is about a child and a book.

After it, read Brontë's Villette (1853), which is colder, stranger and less comforting.
612:
The first Sherlock Holmes story does not begin with Holmes. It begins with Dr John Watson's CV: a medical degree in 1878, army training at Netley, a posting to India, an injury in Afghanistan, and a return to London with little money. Doyle uses a returning invalid, a lodger needing a flatmate, to make the reader meet the detective by accident, which is how most of us meet interesting people.

A Study in Scarlet appeared in Beeton's Christmas Annual in 1887 and has an odd shape. The first part is the London investigation, and the second jumps to the American West and a story of Mormon settlers in Utah, which explains the crime. Readers who enjoy the clues tend to find the long flashback frustrating, and Doyle never again structured a Holmes novel that way.

Doyle himself trained as a doctor at the University of Edinburgh, and one of his teachers, Dr Joseph Bell, is often cited as a model for Holmes's close observation. The opening makes Watson's profession as important as the detective's.

It is also a book that tells you how the partnership began, which later stories assume.

Follow it with The Sign of the Four (1890), where Holmes is more fully himself.
613:
Breakfast, a walking stick and a deduction. The Hound of the Baskervilles starts in the sitting room at Baker Street with Holmes examining a stick left behind by a visitor, Dr Mortimer, and Watson trying his own hand at reading the man from it. Watson gets some of it wrong. This is the series' basic pleasure in small: Holmes explaining, with a slightly unfair advantage, what the rest of us missed.

The novel ran in The Strand Magazine from August 1901 to April 1902. Doyle had killed Holmes off in "The Final Problem" in 1893, and he set this book earlier, in 1889, so that he did not have to bring his detective back from the dead. He said he based the legend of the hound on a Dartmoor tradition told to him by his friend Fletcher Robinson, and the setting, the moor itself, is as important as any character.

For most of the middle of the book Holmes is away from the page. Watson holds the narration and the fear.

If you have read the short stories, this is the best long case. For more of them, try The Return of Sherlock Holmes (1905), the collection that brought him back.
614:
A death is reported before anyone's name is attached to a motive. "Mrs. Ferrars died on the night of the 16th–17th September—a Thursday." The date and weekday are precise, in the way of a notice in a local paper, and it is the narrator's neighbourly, slightly gossipy voice that carries it.

Agatha Christie published The Murder of Roger Ackroyd in 1926. The village is King's Abbot, the narrator is the local doctor, James Sheppard, and Hercule Poirot has recently retired to grow vegetable marrows next door. When the book appeared, its plan caused a public argument about whether a detective story may do what this one does. No explanation of the argument is possible without spoiling the book, so it is worth reading it with that in mind and without looking it up first.

Christie wrote with the reader's habits in view. The opening is domestic and low-key, but the date and the day of the week already look like evidence.

Because it was published in 1926, it entered the public domain in the United States in 2022.

If you'd like another early Christie, try The Secret Adversary (1922), a lighter thriller with Tommy and Tuppence.
615:
The Count of Monte Cristo begins with a ship coming into port. A lookout at the Notre-Dame de la Garde church in Marseille signals the three-master Pharaon, and the date, 24 February 1815, is given before anything else. It is the sort of line that could come from a newspaper's shipping column, and the effect is to start the novel in the world of trade and weather rather than romance.

The precision matters because the plot depends on timing. Young Edmond Dantès is the Pharaon's mate and is about to be promoted and married, and a brief stop at Elba, where Napoleon is in exile, is turned by jealous rivals into an accusation of treason. Within a few chapters he is in the Château d'If. The book's long revenge story rests on how thoroughly the dates and places have been fixed at the start.

Alexandre Dumas wrote it with a collaborator, Auguste Maquet, and it ran in a Paris newspaper, the Journal des Débats, from 1844 to 1846. Dumas's father was a general in the French revolutionary army and the son of a Haitian slave woman and a French nobleman, and Dumas's views on injustice were personal.

Read The Three Musketeers next if you want something faster.
616:
In her first novel Agatha Christie opens with an apology that the story is already old news. "The Styles Case" has "somewhat subsided" from public interest, and the narrator, Captain Arthur Hastings, is going to tell it again, partly to clear the name of someone who was unfairly suspected. The reader is positioned as someone who has heard half the story already.

Christie wrote The Mysterious Affair at Styles during the First World War, while working in a hospital dispensary, where she gained knowledge of drugs and poisons that the plot uses. Several publishers declined it before John Lane's firm, The Bodley Head, accepted it. It appeared in the United States in 1920 and in Britain the following year. It introduced Hercule Poirot as a Belgian refugee living near Styles Court, an Essex country house, and gave him a narrator-companion in Hastings, a pattern she used again and again.

Hastings narrates in a modest, rather puzzled tone. That is the point: a detective needs someone less quick to explain things to.

It is a good starting point for Christie because it is a complete, compact puzzle, with fair clues.

After it, read The Murder of Roger Ackroyd (1926) for a more daring solution.
617:
The story begins with an ending: the managers of the Paris Opera are about to retire, and the night of their farewell gala is chosen as the day everything starts to unravel. Leroux sets up a reader's expectation of a celebration and then undercuts it with the ghost the staff keep talking about.

Gaston Leroux was a journalist and former lawyer, and he wrote Le Fantôme de l'Opéra as a newspaper serial, which ran in Le Gaulois in 1909 and 1910 before appearing as a book. His preface asserts that the Opera ghost really existed, and the novel's tone, an investigator's reconstruction using interviews and documents, follows that claim. The real building did lend him material. The Palais Garnier opened in 1875, and there is genuinely a body of water beneath it, in a cistern used to keep the foundations stable.

The Gutenberg text is an English translation of the early twentieth century, so some phrasing, like "MM.", is French in origin.

Most people know the story through Andrew Lloyd Webber's musical, but the book is harder and odder: more detective story than romance.

Leroux's earlier novel The Mystery of the Yellow Room (1907) is the place to go for his plotting.
618:
A parent's advice, delivered in the first line and followed by a promise not to explain it. Nick Carraway says that his father told him something "that I've been turning over in my mind ever since", and the next lines give the advice itself: when you feel like criticising anyone, remember that not everyone has had your advantages. Nick then proceeds to tell the story of a man he claims not to judge.

That is the book's balancing act. Nick is both a participant and an observer, and he insists on his tolerance while quietly making judgements throughout. The opening hands the reader a standard to test him against.

F. Scott Fitzgerald published The Great Gatsby with Scribner's in April 1925. It sold modestly, and Fitzgerald died in 1940 thinking his best-known book had failed. Its fortunes changed during the Second World War, when around 150,000 copies were distributed free to servicemen in special paperback editions, and by the 1950s it was being taught in schools. It entered the US public domain in 2021.

The "younger and more vulnerable years" phrase also tells you the story is being recalled by an older Nick, which gives the book's lyricism a shade of regret.

Fitzgerald's first novel, This Side of Paradise (1920), is a good contrast: more exuberant, less controlled.
619:
By the end of its first paragraph the novel has told you that someone will be killed. Dostoevsky introduces Alexey Karamazov as "the third son of Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov", a landowner remembered locally for his "gloomy and tragic death" thirteen years before the story's present. The narrator, who speaks like a provincial chronicler, treats the father as the person worth describing and leaves the nominal hero, Alyosha, until later.

The Brothers Karamazov appeared in The Russian Messenger from 1879 to 1880 and is Dostoevsky's last novel. He died in February 1881, a few months after it was published in book form, and said he intended a sequel following Alyosha later in life. The book is a murder case, a family drama and a long argument about faith and doubt, including the chapter "The Grand Inquisitor", which is often read on its own.

The transliteration in this Gutenberg text, "Fyodorovitch", reflects older English conventions. Modern translations spell the same names "Fyodorovich".

Because the first paragraph is mostly a genealogy, it may feel slow, but the nasty father figure it describes is the engine of the whole plot.

Dostoevsky's shorter Notes from Underground is a quicker way into his thinking.
620:
Before there is a character there are smells. The Picture of Dorian Gray opens in a painter's studio with the "rich odour of roses" and the "heavy scent of the lilac", while Lord Henry Wotton lies on a divan. It is a deliberately luxurious scene, and it establishes the aesthetic atmosphere of the book before the plot's moral question arrives.

Oscar Wilde's only novel was published first in Lippincott's Monthly Magazine in 1890. The editors made cuts to the text before printing it, and reviewers were hostile to what they saw as immorality. Wilde responded by expanding it for book publication in 1891, adding several chapters and a preface containing aphorisms, among them "There is no such thing as a moral or an immoral book." Parts of the novel were quoted against him in court during his 1895 trials.

The setting is London in the late nineteenth century, among drawing rooms and clubs. The opening is a still-life and the story goes dark gradually.

Wilde borrowed an idea from J.-K. Huysmans's À rebours (1884), a French novel about an aesthete who retreats from the world. It is referred to in Dorian Gray as a "yellow book" that changes the hero's life.

Wilde's fairy stories, such as "The Happy Prince", show the same wit in a gentler mode.
621:
Hemingway's first paragraph is a description of a place and has no human action in it, and yet it is among the most imitated openings in American fiction. "In the late summer of that year we lived in a house in a village that looked across the river and the plain to the mountains." Notice what is missing: the year is never specified, the narrator is just "we", and the war is only implied by the soldiers who march along the road, raising dust that coats the leaves.

The short, repeating sentences, joined with "and", carry a mood of watching and waiting. Frederic Henry, an American volunteer in the Italian ambulance service, is the narrator, and he speaks of the war with the flatness of someone who has been trained not to react.

A Farewell to Arms was published by Scribner's in 1929. The ending was rewritten many times: in an interview with The Paris Review in 1958, Hemingway said he had rewritten the last page thirty-nine times to get the words right. The novel's setting, Italy in 1916 to 1918, draws on his own service as an ambulance driver on the Italian front.

It entered the US public domain in 2025.

After it, try The Sun Also Rises (1926), which has a similar style in a different setting.
622:
The year first, then a man congratulating himself on his isolation. "1801.—I have just returned from a visit to my landlord—the solitary neighbour that I shall be troubled with." The narrator, Mr Lockwood, is a city gentleman who has rented Thrushcross Grange, and he calls the isolation "a perfect misanthropist's heaven", unaware that he has just introduced the book's most difficult man: Heathcliff.

Opening in a diary entry with a date gives the story a documentary frame, and it is a misleading one. Lockwood is a poor judge of people, and soon he hands the narration over to his housekeeper, Nelly Dean, who tells the long story of the two houses and two generations. The layering of narrators is why readers argue about what actually happened and whom to believe.

Emily Brontë published Wuthering Heights in December 1847 under the name Ellis Bell, in a set with her sister Anne's Agnes Grey. Reviewers found it disturbing and coarse. She died in December 1848, and it is her only novel.

The Yorkshire moorland that the book describes is a presence in every scene.

Her sister Anne's The Tenant of Wildfell Hall (1848) has a nested narrative too and is worth reading alongside it.
623:
The most quoted opening in English is a list of opposites, and it is also an argument. "It was the best of times, it was the worst of times" runs through wisdom and foolishness, belief and incredulity, light and darkness, hope and despair, before Dickens states the point: the period was so like the present one that its noisiest authorities insisted on describing it only in superlatives, for good or evil.

That last clause is often cut when the line is quoted. It turns the sentence from a poetic flourish into a remark on how people talk about their own time.

A Tale of Two Cities was published weekly in Dickens's magazine All the Year Round from April to November 1859. It is set in London and Paris, between 1775 and the French Revolution, and is one of his two historical novels. Dickens acknowledged a debt to Thomas Carlyle's history The French Revolution, and he is said to have read it many times.

Compared with most of his work, it is short and tightly plotted, with few of the comic minor characters that fill his London novels.

If you want a Dickens with more of his usual comedy and a strong sense of place, try Great Expectations or Bleak House.
624:
A king with a garden and a tree of golden apples: one sentence, and the folktale machinery is running. Someone is stealing the apples, and it will be the king's youngest son who stays awake to find out who. The story is "The Golden Bird", from the Grimm collection, and its opening is typical of the form. It sets a rule, a loss, and a duty in a few lines, with no description of what anyone feels.

The brothers Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm published the first volume of their Kinder- und Hausmärchen in 1812. They gathered tales from friends and acquaintances, many of them educated women, and revised the book through seven editions up to 1857. Wilhelm in particular made the language smoother and added more explicit moral turns. The first edition was meant partly as scholarship about German folk culture, and was not written specifically for children, which led them to adjust later printings.

You will notice that the tales are blunt and violent in the way oral stories often are. The Gutenberg edition here is an English translation, and translators have always taken different views of how much of that bluntness to keep.

For a more literary kind of fairy tale, read Hans Christian Andersen's.
625:
The Metamorphosis states the impossible event in its first sentence and then gets on with the day. Gregor Samsa wakes up as a "monstrous vermin" (the German word, Ungeziefer, is vaguer than the English and does not name a species of insect), and the next paragraphs are mostly about the problem of getting out of bed and being late for work. The calm, administrative tone is Kafka's trademark.

Kafka wrote the story in late 1912 and it was first published in 1915. When his publisher considered putting an illustration of the creature on the cover, Kafka wrote to say the insect itself should not be drawn. What he wanted was for the reader to imagine it, or not, and to see only the family's reaction.

That reaction is the real story. Over three parts, the Samsa household moves from shock to practical adjustment to impatience, and the creature in the bedroom who once paid the rent is gradually treated as an inconvenience.

Kafka lived and worked in Prague, writing in German, and held an office job in an insurance institute while writing at night.

His unfinished novel The Trial (1925) is the next stop for a longer taste of the same logic.
626:
It starts mid-conversation, in July 1805, at a soirée in St Petersburg. Anna Pavlovna Scherer is greeting a prince with a political remark about Napoleon's annexation of Genoa and Lucca, which she calls "family estates of the Buonapartes". In the Russian original the first sentence is in French, the language of the aristocratic salon, which tells you immediately who is talking and in what world.

Tolstoy is introducing a society that speaks in a foreign tongue about a war that has not yet touched it. Within a few chapters the story follows families like the Bolkonskys and Rostovs, and a cast of well over a hundred named characters across Russia during the Napoleonic wars. The war arrives from the outside, and the opening party is the last place where the characters are comfortable.

War and Peace appeared in instalments from 1865, and Tolstoy revised the whole thing for its full edition in 1869. The Gutenberg text here is the Louise and Aylmer Maude translation.

Readers often fear the length. The first chapters are social comedy and easy to follow, and the large scale becomes manageable character by character.

For a shorter Tolstoy, read The Death of Ivan Ilyich (1886).
627:
Austen opens with a family history and a house. "The family of Dashwood had long been settled in Sussex." It sounds like a land registry, and it is meant to: the first chapter explains who owns Norland Park, who will inherit it, and why the women of the family will end up with very little. Money and entail are the plot before any love interest appears.

Sense and Sensibility was her first published novel, in October 1811, credited only to "a Lady". Austen paid the risk of publication herself, an arrangement in which the author covers any loss. She had first written it as a series of letters, called "Elinor and Marianne", in the 1790s, and reworked it later. The narrator shifts between the two sisters, one sensible and reserved, the other emotional and impulsive, and the novel gradually complicates both labels.

The first chapter is practical, even grim: a man dies, his son promises to look after his stepmother and half-sisters, and his wife talks him out of it, one sensible-sounding argument after another. It is among the funniest passages in Austen and also the cruellest.

Persuasion (1817), her last finished novel, is a quieter and more mature companion piece.
628:
The first thing the Iliad names is anger. In Greek, the poem opens with the word "mēnin", "wrath", and the whole epic is about the consequences of one man's rage, Achilles, at a slight from his commander Agamemnon. The Muse is asked to sing it.

The version here is Alexander Pope's English translation, published between 1715 and 1720 in heroic couplets, which is why the lines rhyme and why the phrasing, "the direful spring of woes unnumber'd", is so ornate. Pope's Iliad was a commercial success, and it made him financially independent, but it is a very eighteenth-century poem, closer to Pope's own style than to Homer's.

The Iliad does not tell the whole Trojan War. It begins in the tenth year and covers a few weeks, ending with the funeral of Hector, and so it does not include the wooden horse or the fall of Troy. The shape of the story is stated in the first lines and then trusts the audience to know the rest.

The dates of composition are uncertain. Scholars generally place the poem in the late eighth or early seventh century BCE, after a long oral tradition.

Pope's translation of the Odyssey is a natural next read.
629:
The shortest opening in the set: a name, shouted. "TOM!" The first line of the book is a woman calling for a boy who is not answering, and the next lines have Aunt Polly looking under the bed, then out of the window, then into the garden. We learn about Tom Sawyer from the evidence of his absence before we see him.

Mark Twain published The Adventures of Tom Sawyer in 1876. Twain's preface says that most of the adventures recorded in the book really happened, some to himself and the rest to schoolmates, and the town, St Petersburg, Missouri, is a fictional version of Hannibal, where he grew up on the Mississippi. The book is episodic: whitewashing a fence, a graveyard murder witnessed at night, getting lost in a cave.

Twain meant it for boys but also wrote it for the adults who had been boys, and the narrator's tone is half affection, half teasing. It sold steadily rather than spectacularly in its first years.

A single word of dialogue also shows how fast Twain moves. There is no scene-setting, no weather, and no explanation of who Tom is.

The sequel, Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (1884), is darker and the better-known book.
630:
L. Frank Baum was explicit about what he wanted, and he said so in the introduction. He wrote that he hoped to write a modernised fairy tale "in which the wonderment and joy are retained and the heartaches and nightmares are left out". The Wonderful Wizard of Oz begins accordingly with something plain: Dorothy, her aunt and uncle, a farm.

The paragraph that follows, though, is not so cheerful. Baum goes on to describe the grey of the Kansas prairie, grey house, grey grass, and even Aunt Em, who has grown grey and thin. The colour of the opening is part of the point, since the land of Oz is where colour appears.

The book was published in 1900 by George M. Hill, with illustrations by W. W. Denslow, and became a bestseller. Readers who know only the 1939 film may be surprised by differences: Dorothy's magic shoes are silver in the book, not ruby, and the journey to the Emerald City is longer.

Baum went on to write thirteen more Oz books. The next one, The Marvelous Land of Oz (1904), brings back the Scarecrow and introduces a boy named Tip.

The style is clear and brisk, and a good example of children's writing that does not talk down.
631:
Frances Hodgson Burnett does not hide that her heroine is hard to like. "When Mary Lennox was sent to Misselthwaite Manor to live with her uncle everybody said she was the most disagreeable-looking child ever seen." The second half of the sentence matters: it is what everybody said. The narrator has not yet decided, and the following pages explain how a child who was ignored by servants in India has become sour, sallow and tyrannical.

The Secret Garden was serialised in The American Magazine in 1910 and 1911 and published as a book in 1911. Burnett was a successful author who had already written Little Lord Fauntleroy, and she was a keen gardener; she is known to have had a walled rose garden at her house in Kent, Great Maytham Hall, which is often connected with the book.

The novel moves from the colonial India of Mary's early childhood to the Yorkshire moors, and its subject is recovery: of a child, a boy shut in a bedroom, and a neglected plot. The plot is gentle and the cure is practical, not mystical, apart from the garden's effect on everyone who enters it.

For another Burnett, try A Little Princess (1905), which also begins with a girl sent away from India.
632:
The first sentence gives an address. "Mr. Phileas Fogg lived, in 1872, at No. 7, Saville Row, Burlington Gardens." Jules Verne then adds that Sheridan had died in the same house, and the text here gives that date as 1814. Most sources give Richard Brinsley Sheridan's death in 1816, so the slip may be Verne's or a translator's. It is a small instance of how the book likes to anchor itself in checkable details.

Fogg himself is the opposite of an adventurer: a man who keeps exact habits, is described as having been seen nowhere in society, and whose only known pastime is playing whist. That contrast gives the story its comedy, because the wager he makes at the Reform Club, to travel around the world in eighty days for £20,000, turns a perfectly regular man into a racer.

Around the World in Eighty Days came out in 1873, first in the newspaper Le Temps. Part of its premise was topical: new railways and steamship routes, including the Suez Canal opened in 1869, had made such a journey plausible.

Verne's Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea is the obvious next book, though it is more serious in tone.
633:
Huckleberry Finn begins by talking about another book. "You don't know about me without you have read a book by the name of The Adventures of Tom Sawyer; but that ain't no matter." Huck's first move is to correct Twain's earlier novel: he says it was mainly true, with some stretchers, and that he has told the truth himself, except for a few things.

Before that, though, readers meet two short notices. One is a "Notice" that persons attempting to find a motive, a moral or a plot in the narrative will be prosecuted, banished or shot. The other, an "Explanatory", lists the several dialects used, and says that they were not done "by guess-work". They indicate that the voice of the book is the main concern.

Mark Twain published it in Britain in 1884 and in the United States in 1885. The first-person narration, in a Missouri vernacular, was unusual for American fiction at the time, and many later writers have pointed to it as the model for an American literary voice. The book's treatment of race, and its use of a racial slur many times, has also made it a long-running subject of debate in schools.

For Twain's memories of the same river, read Life on the Mississippi (1883).
634:
The first sentence is a survivor's. "Looking back to all that has occurred to me since that eventful day, I am scarcely able to believe in the reality of my adventures." Axel, the young narrator, is already home and is already doubtful, so the reader gets a reason to read: someone who has seen something unlikely and wants to be believed.

Jules Verne published Voyage au centre de la Terre in 1864, as part of the Voyages extraordinaires series for the publisher Pierre-Jules Hetzel. The story starts in Hamburg with Axel's uncle, Professor Lidenbrock, finding a coded note in an old book, in runic letters, that records the route of an Icelandic alchemist, Arne Saknussemm, into the earth through the crater of Snæfellsjökull. Much of the book's fun is in its procedure: Verne takes the reader through the code, the equipment and the descent in a spirit of scientific adventure, and the geology reflects the beliefs of the 1860s.

Verne's first novel in the series was Five Weeks in a Balloon (1863), and this was his second.

The characters are a short cast, a bad-tempered professor, a cautious nephew and a calm Icelandic guide named Hans, and the arguments among them keep the story human.

From the Earth to the Moon (1865) is the next in the same spirit.
635:
A question about whether the narrator will be the hero of his own life. "Whether I shall turn out to be the hero of my own life, or whether that station will be held by anybody else, these pages must show." It is a modest, ironic sentence from a man who is about to tell you about his childhood in detail, and it frames the whole novel as a test of character rather than a series of events.

David Copperfield was published in monthly parts from May 1849 to November 1850. It was the first of Dickens's novels told in the first person, and in a later preface he called it his "favourite child". Parts of the book draw on his own life, especially David's miserable time working in a bottling warehouse as a boy, which mirrors Dickens's months in a blacking factory when his father was in debtors' prison. He kept that episode private for most of his life.

The initials D.C. are Dickens's own reversed, a coincidence he apparently noticed, but one that most editions point out. The story begins before David is born, with his aunt Betsey Trotwood.

The book is long, and the pleasure is in its minor characters, Micawber above all.

For a darker view of the same ground, try Great Expectations.
636:
Anne of Green Gables starts with someone else. The book is named for a girl, and its first words are about a neighbour, "Mrs. Rachel Lynde", who sits at her window watching the road. She is the village's gossip, and her watching sets up the plot: she notices that Matthew Cuthbert is driving out in his good clothes and wonders why.

The long sentence describing where Mrs Lynde's house is, "just where the Avonlea main road dipped down into a little hollow, fringed with alders and ladies' eardrops", is also a statement about the place. Lucy Maud Montgomery grew up on Prince Edward Island, in Cavendish, and Avonlea is its fictional version. She put the setting and its small-community manners at the centre of the book.

It was her first novel, published by L. C. Page of Boston in 1908. She wrote later that the manuscript was rejected by several publishers before it was accepted. It sold well immediately, and she wrote sequels for the rest of her career.

Anne herself arrives in the second chapter, a talkative eleven-year-old orphan who was supposed to be a boy.

Anne of Avonlea (1909) continues the story, and Emily of New Moon (1923) is a darker book by the same author.
637:
"Pip" is a name made by a baby who could not pronounce anything longer. Dickens opens Great Expectations with the narrator explaining where his name came from: his father's family name was Pirrip, his Christian name Philip, and his "infant tongue" reduced them both to "Pip". Typically, the book begins with an act of self-naming, because Pip's central problem later is the question of who he has made himself into.

Pip narrates as an adult, looking back, and the voice has a tone of amused regret. The opening chapter moves quickly from this joke to the churchyard in the Kent marshes, where a convict grabs him by the legs, and the story turns. The contrast between the comic start and the frightening scene is the novel's main method.

Great Expectations was published in weekly instalments in All the Year Round from December 1860 to August 1861. Dickens first wrote an unhappy ending and then changed it at the suggestion of his friend, the novelist Edward Bulwer-Lytton. Both endings are printed in some editions.

It is one of the shorter and tighter of the late novels, and an easier introduction to Dickens than most.

Oliver Twist (1838) is a rougher, earlier take on a poor orphan's rise.
638:
The narrator offers to tell you everything but the location. Jim Hawkins says he has been asked to write down "the whole particulars about Treasure Island, from the beginning to the end, keeping nothing back but the bearings of the island". It is a promise and a refusal at the same time, and it makes the reader complicit in a secret, as if we might be the next treasure hunters.

Robert Louis Stevenson began the story in 1881, at a rented cottage in Scotland, by drawing a map of an imaginary island for his stepson, Lloyd Osbourne, and then writing a chapter a day to read aloud. It first ran in the magazine Young Folks as "The Sea-Cook, or Treasure Island" under the pen name Captain George North, and came out as a book in 1883.

Stevenson's pirates set the pattern for many later ones: the black spot, the one-legged sea cook with a parrot who screams "pieces of eight", the treasure map marked with an X. Much of what we think of as pirate lore comes from this book.

The tale is narrated by a boy, so the violence is seen from a boy's level and softened by his sense of adventure.

For more Stevenson, try Kidnapped (1886), set in the Scotland of the Jacobite risings.
639:
"Once upon a time there were four little Rabbits, and their names were—Flopsy, Mopsy, Cotton-tail, and Peter." The dash before the list gives the sentence a small pause, a reader's breath, and Peter is named last so that he can be the subject of everything that follows.

Beatrix Potter first told the story in a picture letter in 1893 to Noel Moore, the young son of her former governess, who was ill. In 1901 she printed 250 copies of the tale privately after publishers turned it down, and in 1902 Frederick Warne & Co. brought out a trade edition with colour plates. The small format was deliberate. She wanted it to fit a child's hand.

The narration is very economical, with short sentences and a dry tone. Peter's mother tells him not to go into Mr. McGregor's garden because his father had an accident there and was "put in a pie by Mrs. McGregor", and the book does not comment on this.

Her paintings of plants and animals were drawn from careful study, and she was also a serious student of fungi.

The Tale of Squirrel Nutkin (1903) is a good next book, with a more mischievous main character.
640:
The Importance of Being Earnest does not open with a line at all. It opens with a stage direction: "Morning-room in Algernon's flat in Half-Moon Street." What follows is a quiet comic scene in which Algernon plays the piano offstage and his butler, Lane, answers questions about cucumber sandwiches and champagne with perfect composure. The play's joke is that no one will show surprise at anything.

Wilde called it "a trivial comedy for serious people". It premiered at the St James's Theatre in London on 14 February 1895, and for a short while Wilde had two successes running in the West End. Within weeks of the opening, however, the Marquess of Queensberry's accusations led to Wilde's prosecution and imprisonment, and the production closed. The play was published in 1899.

It was first written in four acts and cut to three at the request of the actor-manager George Alexander. The surviving text is therefore tightly built, with the pleasure of its paradoxes arriving on a regular beat.

Reading it, notice how Wilde gives servants and aristocrats the same style of speech, so that even the butler is witty.

Next, read Lady Windermere's Fan (1892), a comedy with a more serious side, or Sheridan's The School for Scandal (1777), a predecessor.
641:
Two men are drinking wine and arranging a sale, and the sale is a human being. Harriet Beecher Stowe starts Uncle Tom's Cabin in a Kentucky dining room, "late in the afternoon of a chilly day in February", with the owner, Mr Shelby, and a slave trader, Haley, talking business in the language of ordinary commerce. The politeness of the scene is the argument. Nothing in the dialogue is shouted, and the reader understands the horror because the speakers do not.

The town is given as "P——", with a dash. That was a convention of the period, a nod to realism that also kept real places vague, and it appears throughout nineteenth-century novels.

Stowe's novel was serialised in the anti-slavery newspaper The National Era between 1851 and 1852 and published as a book in March 1852. It sold in very large numbers on both sides of the Atlantic, and was among the best-selling books of the century. It was also attacked in the South, and an entire genre of "anti-Tom" novels appeared in reply. The book's characters, particularly Tom, later became stereotypes in popular theatre, in ways Stowe did not intend.

For a first-hand account that sits alongside it, read Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass (1845), which is available on Gutenberg.
642:
Barrie's opening line states the whole philosophy of the book in five words: "All children, except one, grow up." It is followed by a quick scene in which Wendy, aged two, picks a flower and runs to her mother, and her mother says she wishes she could stay that way. That is the moment, the text says, when Wendy knew she must grow up.

The text on Gutenberg is the novel, published in 1911 as Peter and Wendy. It came after the stage play Peter Pan, first performed in London on 27 December 1904. Peter himself first appeared in a section of Barrie's earlier novel The Little White Bird (1902). Barrie was inspired in part by the five sons of his friends Arthur and Sylvia Llewelyn Davies, whom he came to know in Kensington Gardens.

In 1929 Barrie gave the rights to Peter Pan to Great Ormond Street Hospital for Children in London, which has benefited from it since. In the UK, that arrangement has a special legal exception.

The book is sadder and odder than most adaptations: Peter forgets people quickly, and the narrator comments openly on how little children's feelings last.

The Little White Bird shows Barrie at his most whimsical and is the place to find Peter's first appearance.
643:
"Marley was dead: to begin with." The colon and the clipped "to begin with" make it sound like a lawyer's opening statement. The following sentence insists, "There is no doubt whatever about that", and the narrator goes on at some length about the signed register and the undertaker. Dickens wants the corpse established as fact so that what happens next, a ghost in chains, lands as a shock.

A Christmas Carol was published in December 1843 by Chapman & Hall, with illustrations by John Leech. Dickens had arranged the production himself, and he was disappointed at first by how little profit it made, because the book was costly to make. It still sold out its first printing within days. He divided it into "staves", as in verses of a song, rather than chapters.

The story is short, around thirty thousand words, and is readable in an evening. Dickens also performed it publicly, in an abridged form, in his later years, and made the readings one of his most popular events.

Scrooge's world is fixed in exact detail: his clerk Bob Cratchit's coal, the single candle, the counting-house door. The ghosts come later, but the specificity of the opening is the reason they work.

Dickens wrote more Christmas books, and The Chimes (1844) is the one most like this.
644:
A date in the past, calculated as if the reader were doing arithmetic. "Three hundred and forty-eight years, six months, and nineteen days ago to-day, the Parisians awoke to the sound of all the bells..." Victor Hugo counts back from his own time, the book was published in 1831, to 1482, and the effect is a piece of mock-precision that places the reader inside a living Paris of the late Middle Ages.

The novel's French title is Notre-Dame de Paris, and its real subject is the cathedral. Hugo wanted to draw attention to Gothic buildings, which many Parisians then treated as old and unfashionable, and a chapter of the book is devoted to a description of Paris from the top of the towers. The "hunchback" in the English title, Quasimodo, is a figure within that building, not its focus.

The book was a popular success and is often credited with helping build support for the cathedral's restoration, which began in the 1840s under the architect Eugène Viollet-le-Duc.

The first scene is a medieval mystery play interrupted by the crowd, an odd and rowdy start for a novel that eventually turns tragic.

Hugo's Les Misérables (1862) is the bigger, later book.
645:
Virginia Woolf begins with a decision and an errand. "Mrs. Dalloway said she would buy the flowers herself." The sentence is plain, but it sets up a book told from inside a single mind over a single day, and the day starts with a woman choosing to do a small thing on her own.

The novel is set in London on a Wednesday in June 1923. Clarissa Dalloway is preparing for an evening party, and the book follows her through the day while moving, sometimes mid-sentence, to other people nearby, among them Septimus Smith, a veteran suffering from the aftermath of the First World War. Big Ben's chimes mark the hours and tie the separate lives together. Woolf's method, called stream of consciousness, mixes thought and description without conventional signposts.

Mrs Dalloway appeared in 1925 from Hogarth Press, the small publishing house Woolf ran with her husband Leonard. It grew out of a short story, "Mrs Dalloway in Bond Street", which she had published in 1923, and Clarissa had also appeared in her first novel, The Voyage Out (1915).

Its first line is easy to read, and the book gets more intricate afterwards.

Her next novel, To the Lighthouse (1927), is the place to go for more.
646:
The Time Traveller has no name, and the narrator apologises for it. "The Time Traveller (for so it will be convenient to speak of him) was expounding a recondite matter to us." The parenthesis is a small act of misdirection: it presents an unbelievable story as the account of a guest at a dinner party, a man whose name the writer is not going to supply.

H. G. Wells used the frame to ease readers into science fiction. At first the Traveller lectures his friends on four dimensions, and shows them a small model. The audience politely doubts him. A week later he turns up late, dishevelled, and tells them of a world in the year 802,701 populated by the gentle Eloi and the underground Morlocks. The frame then lets the reader decide whether to believe him.

The Time Machine was Wells's first novel, published by Heinemann in 1895 after a serial in the New Review. He had written an earlier version as a story called "The Chronic Argonauts" in 1888, in a college magazine.

The book is short, brisk, and political: Wells's picture of the far future is also a comment on the class divisions of Victorian England.

For another early Wells, try The Island of Doctor Moreau (1896).
647:
Tolstoy's first sentence is so often quoted that it can obscure its position in the book. "Happy families are all alike; every unhappy family is unhappy in its own way." The next line is blunt and domestic: "Everything was in confusion in the Oblonskys' house." The aphorism is not an essay topic; it introduces a household where the husband's affair has just been discovered.

That house is not Anna Karenina's. She arrives a few chapters later, to help mend her brother's marriage, and her own unhappiness follows. The novel runs two stories in parallel, Anna's and Konstantin Levin's, and the contrast between a doomed love and a slowly achieved marriage is where the book gets its shape. Before chapter one, Tolstoy places an epigraph from the Bible: "Vengeance is mine; I will repay."

Anna Karenina was serialised from 1875 to 1877 in The Russian Messenger and published as a book in 1878. It is set in the 1870s, among Moscow and St Petersburg society and a country estate.

Many translations render the opening in slightly different ways; the Gutenberg text here is one of the earlier English versions.

Tolstoy's late novella The Death of Ivan Ilyich (1886) is shorter and just as concerned with how a life is lived.
648:
Les Misérables begins with a bishop, not the convict. The long novel, published in 1862, opens in the year 1815 with Charles-François-Bienvenu Myriel, Bishop of D——, an old man of seventy-five. Hugo then spends the entire first book describing him: his income, his habits, his house, and the way he gave most of his salary to the poor. The convict Jean Valjean does not appear until the second book.

That is a bold choice for a novel with a famous central character, but it has a purpose. Valjean is rescued from despair by the bishop's act of mercy, and Hugo wants the reader to understand the kind of man who could do it before the story depends on it.

The names in the opening are shortened with dashes, "D——", which was a common nineteenth-century device, but here it also serves the book's habit of mixing fictional characters with real history. The setting runs from 1815 to the 1832 Paris uprising.

Hugo wrote parts of the book in exile on the Channel Islands after he left France following Napoleon III's coup in 1851. It is long, with essays on the Battle of Waterloo, the Paris sewers and convent life.

For something shorter by the same author, try The Last Day of a Condemned Man (1829).
649:
The dog in this story does not know he is in danger, and the narrator does. "Buck did not read the newspapers, or he would have known that trouble was brewing." The irony is dry and slightly amused, a human narrator looking at an animal protagonist and explaining the news he is missing: gold has been found in the Klondike, and strong dogs are suddenly worth money.

Jack London published The Call of the Wild in 1903, and it made his name. He had himself travelled to the Yukon in 1897 and 1898, during the gold rush, and spent a winter in the north. He took from that experience the details of cold, sled harness and hunger. Buck, a large dog living comfortably on a California estate, is stolen and sold into the north, where he must adapt to survive.

The book is told in third person, but it keeps close to Buck's perceptions and avoids giving him human speech. London was criticised by some contemporaries for making animals too thoughtful, and he answered in print.

It is under 35,000 words and very easy to read in one sitting.

The companion book, White Fang (1906), runs the other way: a wolf-dog who is gradually tamed.
650:
The first sentence is a compliment with a catch. "Emma Woodhouse, handsome, clever, and rich, with a comfortable home and happy disposition, seemed to unite some of the best blessings of existence". The word that matters is "seemed", and the clause that follows, "had lived nearly twenty-one years in the world with very little to distress or vex her", is a quiet warning. A character with nothing to trouble her has had nothing to teach her.

Emma was published in December 1815 (the title page says 1816) by John Murray, and is dedicated to the Prince Regent. Austen's nephew recorded her remark that she was going to take a heroine "whom no one but myself will much like". The book is notable for its formal technique: it follows Emma's point of view so closely that the reader is misled by her mistakes along with her, and the clues to the plot are in plain sight.

The setting is a single village, Highbury, in Surrey, and almost the whole story takes place within a few miles of it.

It is Austen's longest novel and her most structurally clever.

Persuasion, her last complete book, is the companion in a quieter, more rueful key.
651:
Jo is lying on the rug and complaining. "Christmas won't be Christmas without any presents," she says, and the reply from the other sisters is part sigh and part laughter. In the course of a few lines Louisa May Alcott gives us the four March girls: Jo, Meg, Beth and Amy, each with a different tone of voice. It's an economical introduction to a family.

Little Women appeared in two volumes, in 1868 and 1869, and Alcott wrote it at the suggestion of her publisher Thomas Niles, who wanted a book for girls. She did not expect much from it. She based the March sisters on herself and her own sisters, and Jo is the version of herself she most admired. It was an immediate success, and the second volume was published in Britain as Good Wives.

The setting is Massachusetts during the American Civil War. The girls' father is away as an army chaplain, and the family is not wealthy. The first chapter shows them deciding to spend their small Christmas money on gifts for their mother, and the story begins with that decision.

For something by Alcott from her own wartime experience, read Hospital Sketches (1863), based on her time as a nurse.
652:
Before anyone speaks, we are on a boat that is not moving. "The Nellie, a cruising yawl, swung to her anchor without a flutter of the sails, and was at rest." Conrad starts with stillness: the Thames estuary at Gravesend, the tide on the turn, five men waiting for the water to change, and one of them, Marlow, about to talk.

Heart of Darkness is a story told inside a story. An unnamed narrator on the Nellie reports what Marlow says, and Marlow recalls a journey up the Congo River to find a trader named Kurtz. The setting of the frame matters: Marlow begins by saying that this place, too, "has been one of the dark places of the earth", reminding his listeners that London was once a colonial frontier for the Romans.

Joseph Conrad, born in Poland and writing in English as his third language, worked on a Congo steamer in 1890, and the book draws on that experience. It was serialised in Blackwood's Magazine in 1899 and published in book form in 1902. The Nigerian writer Chinua Achebe criticised it in a 1975 lecture for its portrayal of Africans, and the argument has since been part of how it is read.

For another Conrad narrated by Marlow, try Lord Jim (1900).
653:
The narrator of Gulliver's Travels sounds like a man who wants to be taken for a plain witness. "My father had a small estate in Nottinghamshire; I was the third of five sons." He gives the practical details of a respectable middle-class man: his education, his apprenticeship to a surgeon, his studies, his marriage. Swift wants the reader to stay with that steady voice for as long as possible before the fantastic begins.

The voice is borrowed from the real travel books of Swift's day, which were popular and often padded. By copying their plain tone, with dates, latitudes and ship names, he made absurd events sound reasonable. Lilliput, the land of six-inch people, is introduced the same way as any real port.

The book was published anonymously in 1726 by Benjamin Motte, who altered the text to avoid offending powerful people. Swift complained about the changes, and later Irish editions restored some of what had been removed. It has four parts, each a voyage: to Lilliput, Brobdingnag, Laputa and its neighbours, and the land of the Houyhnhnms.

Children usually get only the first part. The later parts are more bitter.

Swift's pamphlet A Modest Proposal (1729) is a short, savage example of the same satire.
654:
Kipling starts with a wolf waking up. "It was seven o'clock of a very warm evening in the Seeonee hills when Father Wolf woke up from his day's rest, scratched himself, yawned, and spread out his paws one after the other to get rid of the sleepy feeling in their tips." It is the detail of the paws that makes the sentence work: a specific, observed habit of a real animal, described by someone who has watched.

This is the opening of "Mowgli's Brothers", the first story in The Jungle Book (1894), in which a human baby is found by a wolf family and the tiger Shere Khan comes to claim him. The book mixes the Mowgli stories with other tales, such as "Rikki-Tikki-Tavi", the mongoose, and each story is followed by a short poem.

Rudyard Kipling was born in Bombay and spent his early childhood in India, and he returned there as a young man. He wrote The Jungle Book in Vermont, where he was living with his American wife's family. The Seeonee hills of the story are in central India.

The animals follow what Kipling calls the Law of the Jungle, a code that the stories use to discuss obedience and belonging.

The Second Jungle Book (1895) continues Mowgli's story, and Kim (1901) is Kipling's novel about a boy in India.
655:
The book begins with a puzzle, not with the sea. "The year 1866 was signalised by a remarkable incident, a mysterious and puzzling phenomenon, which doubtless no one has yet forgotten." The narrator, the French naturalist Pierre Aronnax, assumes that the reader has heard about the strange sightings at sea, and the first chapters are an account of ships that have collided with something enormous, which most people think is a giant narwhal.

That setup is typical of Verne. He starts with news reports and scientific speculation, and gradually reveals the cause: Captain Nemo's submarine, the Nautilus. By the time Aronnax is captured, the reader already expects a marine monster, and the machine is the surprise.

Vingt mille lieues sous les mers was serialised in the magazine Magasin d'éducation et de récréation from 1869 and published as a book in 1870. The first English translation, in 1872, was abridged and contained many errors, including changes to scientific details. This shaped English readers' view of Verne as a writer for boys. Modern translations are fuller.

"Twenty thousand leagues" refers to the distance travelled, not the depth.

The sequel, The Mysterious Island (1875), explains more about Nemo's origins.
656:
Cervantes opens with an author who cannot remember. "In a village of La Mancha, the name of which I have no desire to call to mind" is the usual English rendering of "En un lugar de la Mancha, de cuyo nombre no quiero acordarme." It reads like a casual aside, but it sets the book's tone: a narrator who knows where the story begins and prefers to be vague about it.

The sentence goes on to describe the hero, an ageing country gentleman with a lance, a shield, a lean horse and a greyhound, in an inventory of poverty. The weapons are all out of date. Cervantes has described a man whose imagination and his circumstances do not match.

Don Quixote was published in two parts, in 1605 and 1615. Cervantes presents the first part as a translation of a history written by an Arab historian, Cide Hamete Benengeli, and adds other layers of invented authorship. In the second part, characters have read the first part and respond to it, which makes the book an early work of self-reference.

It began as a parody of chivalric romances, then became a much wider study of reading and delusion. The Gutenberg text is an older English translation and keeps some of the formality of its time.

For a short Spanish predecessor in the picaresque style, read Lazarillo de Tormes (1554).
657:
Dickens refuses to name the town, and uses the refusal to be sarcastic. "Among other public buildings in a certain town, which for many reasons it will be prudent to refrain from mentioning, and to which I will assign no fictitious name, there is one anciently common to most towns, great or small: to wit, a workhouse." The sentence waits until its final word to say what the building is, and the delay is the joke.

Oliver Twist was published in monthly instalments in Bentley's Miscellany from 1837 to 1839 and as a three-volume book in 1838, while Dickens was still writing the later chapters. He was in his mid-twenties, and the book was his second novel, following The Pickwick Papers. It was an attack on the Poor Law Amendment Act of 1834, which required the destitute to enter workhouses where conditions were deliberately harsh.

The opening chapter describes the birth of its hero in that workhouse, in language that mimics official reports. The famous scene of the boy asking for more porridge comes a few chapters later.

The mix of satire and melodrama is what makes the book hard to categorise: comic beadles and a very dark crime plot, side by side.

For Dickens at full length on the law and the poor, try Bleak House (1853).
658:
"Here is Edward Bear, coming downstairs now, bump, bump, bump, on the back of his head, behind Christopher Robin." It sounds like someone telling a story to a child, with a pause for the bumps. The sentence says "now", as if the toy is arriving as we speak, which is the way a bedtime story would introduce it.

A. A. Milne wrote Winnie-the-Pooh for his son Christopher Robin, and the book was published in 1926 by Methuen, with drawings by E. H. Shepard. The toys were real ones owned by the Milne family, and Pooh's first name came from a Canadian black bear called Winnipeg, or Winnie, at London Zoo, which Christopher Robin liked to visit. In the story the bear explains that he used to be called Edward Bear but is now called Winnie-the-Pooh.

Milne frames the tales as being told by a narrator to Christopher Robin, who interrupts. That device allows jokes aimed at adults as well as children, and it explains the book's rhythm of short episodes.

The 1926 original entered the US public domain in 2022.

The House at Pooh Corner (1928) is the sequel and has the most poignant ending.
659:
Robinson Crusoe starts like a memoir, and carefully. "I was born in the year 1632, in the city of York, of a good family, though not of that country, my father being a foreigner of Bremen." The year, the city and the father's origin are given as if for a legal record, and Defoe goes on to explain that the family name had been Kreutznaer but was anglicised into Crusoe.

The book was published in April 1719, and the title page described it as the life and strange surprising adventures of a mariner "written by himself". Defoe's name was not on it, and many readers took it as a true account. He was a journalist and pamphleteer, used to writing in a factual manner, and he used the same style to make an unlikely story believable. Crusoe's shipwreck and twenty-eight years on an island are said to have been inspired in part by the real experiences of sailors such as Alexander Selkirk, though the link is debated.

The first paragraphs are about a young man ignoring his father's advice. Crusoe wants to go to sea, his father warns against it, and he goes anyway. The novel treats this disobedience as the origin of everything that follows.

Defoe's Moll Flanders (1722) uses the same first-person method for a woman's rise and fall.
660:
The most famous opening in early science fiction puts humanity under a microscope. "No one would have believed in the last years of the nineteenth century that this world was being watched keenly and closely by intelligences greater than man's and yet as mortal as his own." The sentence continues with men busy about their affairs, like creatures in a drop of water. The perspective is that of a narrator looking back, and the comparison to microscopic life is the sort of image that a Victorian reader would find familiar.

H. G. Wells wrote The War of the Worlds while living in Woking, in Surrey, and sets the first landing on Horsell Common nearby. He later explained that the idea came from a conversation with his brother about what would happen if Martians did to England what Europeans had done to Tasmania. The novel was serialised in Pearson's Magazine in 1897 and published as a book by Heinemann in 1898.

It is told by an unnamed narrator, a writer, and includes his brother's separate account of events in London. The narrator is mostly an observer who survives, as opposed to a hero.

In 1938 Orson Welles adapted it as a radio drama set in New Jersey, which has become part of its legend.

Wells's The First Men in the Moon (1901) is a lighter, more comic scientific romance.
661:
Dumas starts with a riot, or at least with a town that behaves as though it were in one. "On the first Monday of the month of April, 1625, the market town of Meung... appeared to be in as perfect a state of revolution as if the Huguenots had just made a second La Rochelle of it." What has happened is that a young man has arrived on an old yellow horse and been insulted. The scale of the comparison is the joke.

The Three Musketeers was published in 1844, first as a newspaper serial in Le Siècle, and it made Dumas wealthy. He wrote it with the help of Auguste Maquet, who supplied plots and research, and Dumas rewrote them in his own fast, dialogue-heavy style. The central figure, d'Artagnan, was a real person, and Dumas took the idea from a fictional memoir of him published in 1700 by Gatien de Courtilz de Sandras.

The book is set in the France of Louis XIII, with Cardinal Richelieu as the main antagonist. The title is slightly misleading: d'Artagnan is not a musketeer for most of the story, and the three friends, Athos, Porthos and Aramis, take him in.

The sequel, Twenty Years After (1845), picks up the characters in middle age.
662:
Where Alice's first book begins in boredom, the second begins with a cat. "One thing was certain, that the white kitten had had nothing to do with it: it was the black kitten's fault entirely." The sentence jumps in at the end of a quarrel: the kitten is accused of unravelling a ball of wool, and Alice, scolding, is already talking to a world that listens.

Lewis Carroll published Through the Looking-Glass, and What Alice Found There in December 1871, with the date 1872 on the title page. It is built on a chess game: the landscape is divided into squares by brooks and hedges, Alice begins as a pawn and aims to become a queen, and the characters she meets are chess pieces or things that go along with them. It contains the poem "Jabberwocky", whose nonsense words Humpty Dumpty explains in a later chapter.

The kittens, Dinah's two, are called Kitty and Snowdrop in the text. The book's first sentences are a good example of Carroll's habit of making a child's domestic scolding into a miniature of logical argument.

The mirror is the entry point, and the book's reversal motif, walking away to get closer, follows from it.

Carroll's long poem The Hunting of the Snark (1876) is the nonsense verse to read next.
663:
Voltaire starts with a place name designed to sound ridiculous. "In a castle of Westphalia, belonging to the Baron of Thunder-ten-Tronckh, lived a youth, whom nature had endowed with the most gentle manners." The Baron's name is a mock-German tongue-twister, and the youth is called Candide, which in French means candid, or innocent.

The following pages introduce his tutor, Dr Pangloss, who teaches that this is the best of all possible worlds and that everything has a reason. The book then marches Candide through war, earthquake, shipwreck and betrayal in order to test that claim. Pangloss is a parody of the German philosopher Leibniz's optimism, and the novel was written partly in reaction to the Lisbon earthquake of 1755, which killed tens of thousands.

Candide was published in Geneva in 1759 under a made-up title page that described it as translated from the German of a "Doctor Ralph". Voltaire publicly denied that he had written it, though almost nobody was fooled, and it sold in huge numbers despite being banned in some places.

It is short, around forty thousand words, and fast, with a sentence like a punch every few lines.

Samuel Johnson's Rasselas, published in the same year, takes the same question in a gentler way.
664:
The Wind in the Willows begins with housework. "The Mole had been working very hard all the morning, spring-cleaning his little home." The animal is occupied with a human chore, and by the end of the paragraph he has thrown down his brush and walked out, "something up above was calling him", into a spring morning that leads him to the river and to Rat.

That first scene is the book's basic transaction: comfort against the pull of the outdoors. The characters, Mole, Rat, Badger and Toad, have domestic habits and houses, and also a landscape of river, field and Wild Wood. The tone is cosy but not simple. Toad's mania for motor cars and the chapter in which the animals meet the god Pan are both there.

Kenneth Grahame was Secretary of the Bank of England when he wrote it, and it started as bedtime stories and letters he told his son Alastair. Methuen published it in 1908. Early reviews were lukewarm, but the book kept selling, and it became a children's classic in the following decades.

The Shepard illustrations familiar to many readers came later, in an edition from 1931.

Grahame's earlier The Golden Age (1895) is a book of essays about childhood from a child's view.
665:
"Who's there?" is the first line of Hamlet and it is spoken by the wrong person. Bernardo, arriving to relieve the night watch, should be the one challenged. Instead the sentry on duty, Francisco, is the one who asks, and Bernardo replies with an answer, "Nay, answer me. Stand, and unfold yourself." The play begins with both men too nervous to behave normally, and the audience is put on edge at once.

Setting a play at midnight on a castle battlement at Elsinore, in cold and dark, with guards expecting a ghost, is a strong way to start. Shakespeare gets the supernatural out of the way in the first scene, and the rest of the play can then be about what people do about it. The play is also full of questions, from "Who's there?" to "To be, or not to be", and the opening sets that habit.

The text was first printed in 1603 in a short quarto, the so-called First Quarto, which differs a lot from the better-known versions of 1604 and 1623. In it, for instance, the famous soliloquy appears in a different place and different words.

The title role is the longest in Shakespeare, and the play is Shakespeare's longest.

For another Shakespeare tragedy that starts in the supernatural, read Macbeth.
666:
Flaubert begins with "we". "We were in class when the head-master came in, followed by a 'new fellow'." The narrator is a schoolboy, one of the class, and he describes the new boy, Charles Bovary, in the ruthless detail of children who have already decided what they think of him: a country lad in a badly cut jacket, with a ridiculous cap.

The "we" lasts for only a few pages. After the school scenes the narrator disappears, and the novel proceeds in an impersonal third person, which is part of what made Flaubert famous. He aimed at a style in which the author was invisible. Few readers remember that the book starts with a first-person plural narrator who then vanishes.

Madame Bovary was serialised in the Revue de Paris in late 1856 and published as a book in 1857. That year Flaubert was prosecuted for offending public morals and was acquitted. The trial helped to make the book famous. It took him about five years to write, and he is known to have spent days on single pages.

The story concerns Emma Bovary, married to a dull country doctor and devoted to romantic novels. The English text here is an older translation.

Flaubert's later A Sentimental Education (1869) uses a similar technique over a longer span.
667:
Macbeth begins with a question about the weather. "When shall we three meet again? In thunder, lightning, or in rain?" The speakers are three witches, and their arrangement for a future meeting sounds like friends fixing a time. The next lines name the place, a heath, and the person they will meet there: Macbeth.

The scene is only about ten lines long, and the play's most-quoted idea is in the last two: "Fair is foul, and foul is fair." Shakespeare uses the witches to establish that language can be turned inside out. The word "fair" will be echoed by Macbeth himself, in his first entrance, when he says "So foul and fair a day I have not seen."

Macbeth is the shortest of Shakespeare's tragedies. It was probably written around 1606, and it was first printed in the First Folio of 1623. Shakespeare took the story from Holinshed's Chronicles, a sixteenth-century history, and he adjusted it, partly to please King James I, who was supposed to be descended from Banquo and who was interested in witchcraft.

The setting is Scotland in the eleventh century, and the play has an unusual number of references to blood, night and sleep.

Hamlet, also in this archive, is a good counterpart: it is long and reflective, while Macbeth moves fast.
668:
Josef K. is arrested in the first sentence and not told why. "Someone must have been telling lies about Josef K., he knew he had done nothing wrong but, one morning, he was arrested." The structure of the sentence is a small trial in itself: a guess about the cause, a statement of innocence, and then the event, which happens regardless.

The arrest takes place in his rented room, by two men who do not explain themselves, and the rest of the novel follows him as he tries to find out what he is accused of and by whom. He never learns. Kafka's world is full of offices, forms and clerks, and the court sits in an attic over a tenement.

Kafka wrote The Trial in 1914 and 1915 and did not finish it. He told his friend Max Brod to burn his unpublished papers after his death in 1924. Brod ignored the request, arranged the chapters, and published the novel in 1925. The order of the middle chapters is Brod's decision, and later editions have rearranged them.

The Gutenberg text here is a modern English translation by David Wyllie, who has made several Kafka translations freely available.

The Castle, also unfinished and published posthumously in 1926, covers a surveyor who cannot get access to a village's authority.
669:
The Tempest begins in the middle of a storm, and the first voice is a sailor's, not a king's. "Boats. Heigh, my hearts!" The master of the ship calls his boatswain, who shouts orders to the crew, and when the courtiers on board come on deck to complain, he tells them to go below. It's a scene in which rank means nothing against the weather.

The storm turns out to have been conjured by Prospero, the exiled Duke of Milan, who lives on an island with his daughter Miranda and uses magic to bring his enemies to him. The opening scene is a trick: the audience is shown a disaster, and the next scene reveals that nobody has been hurt.

The Tempest was probably written around 1610 or 1611, and it is the first play in the First Folio of 1623, the first collected edition of Shakespeare's plays. Scholars have often linked it to accounts of the wreck of the Sea Venture off Bermuda in 1609, which were widely read in England, although the island in the play is never named.

It is usually counted among Shakespeare's last works written mainly by himself.

The Winter's Tale, from about the same period, is a similar late romance with a long journey and a forgiveness at the end.
